claim: Client Solutions Group is an umbrella term inside Asset Management for everyone who speaks to clients; it is the equivalent of saying "sales".
finding: Goldman's own campus titles read "Client Solutions Group / Sales" (Frankfurt) and "Client Solutions Group (Sales)" (Tokyo), and an internal role refers to "the sales organization" [@R1-S04] [@R1-S09] [@R1-S14]. Goldman's one-paragraph definition says the group develops client relationships and delivers investment solutions for institutional and third-party wealth clients [@R1-S10]. Limit: not everyone who speaks to clients is in it. OCIO investment staff in Multi-Asset Solutions meet clients and sit outside the sales organisation [@R1-S15].
use_in_interview: Safe to say CSG is the firm's client and sales organisation for asset management. Do not say it contains every client-facing person.

claim: It covers three functions: sales, client relationship management and consultant relations.
finding: All three functions exist in Goldman advertisements. A London CSG team does both new business and existing relationships [@R1-S01]; consultant relations works with the regional institutional sales teams [@R1-S21]; a job advertisement lists the channels as third party wealth, institutional, consultant, insurance and retirement [@R4-S09]. No public source gives this exact three-way list as the group's formal structure.
use_in_interview: Use it as a description of the kinds of work, not as an org chart.

claim: The group is cut by coverage team (mostly regional), then by client type, then by sales versus relationship management.
finding: Job advertisements show country or regional teams crossed with channel: for example Institutional Sales in Frankfurt and Third Party Wealth in Paris and Dubai as named CSG sub-tracks [@R1-S05] [@R1-S06] [@R1-S07]. That supports the first two cuts as a matrix. No source shows them as an ordered hierarchy, and no reporting lines are published. The third cut (sales versus relationship management inside each client-type team) is not shown by any public source.
use_in_interview: Describe geography and client type as overlapping cuts. Ask how the team divides new business from existing clients; do not state it.

claim: Most regional teams split into Third Party Wealth and Institutional, like the UK.
finding: Consistent with advertisements for Germany and Austria (Frankfurt institutional sales and a German third-party wealth team) [@R1-S05] [@R5-S07] and Benelux [@R1-S01]. The Nordics are an exception on the public record: in May 2020 third-party distribution and institutional sales were merged into one Nordic organisation [@R5-S26]. Whether that is still so in 2026 was not established.
use_in_interview: Fine as a general pattern with the Nordic exception noted.

claim: The coverage teams are UK, Middle East, Nordics, Switzerland, Benelux, Liquidity Solutions and Insurance, and that list is "everyone". Germany, France, Italy and Iberia were not mentioned.
finding: The list is incomplete for EMEA. Germany and Austria are covered from Frankfurt and France from Paris, both recruiting CSG analysts for 2027 with a local language [@R1-S05] [@R1-S06]. Italy has a country head and Iberia a managing director whose team moved from London to Madrid in 2021 [@R6-S11] [@R6-S12] [@R6-S13]. The likeliest reading is that he listed the teams with seats in London, which is an inference.
use_in_interview: Do not repeat the list as complete. If asked about EMEA coverage, say continental markets are largely covered from local offices.

claim: The UK team is the largest by far, brings in the most money and so should have the best bonus.
finding: Goldman discloses no revenue, assets, flows or headcount for the UK or for any client team. The only regional figure is EMEA assets under supervision of $799bn at 30 September 2026 [@R2-S01] [@R2-S02]. Nothing public supports a ranking of teams or any statement about bonuses.
use_in_interview: Do not use.

topic: UK team: Institutional and Third Party Wealth
claim: The UK team is split by client type into Institutional and Third Party Wealth (and OCIO).
finding: "UK Third Party Wealth (TPW) Sales Team" is Goldman's own wording in a closed London advertisement [@R1-S17]. A 2026-cycle London listing titled "Client Solutions Group, UK Institutional Sales" appears in search results but the page had expired [@R1-S31]. The senior public title is EMEA-wide: "co-head of EMEA Institutional Client Coverage" [@R6-S02]. Whether "UK Institutional" is a formal team name today is not established.
use_in_interview: "Third Party Wealth" can be used as an official name. Say "the UK institutional business" rather than asserting a team name.

claim: OCIO is the third client-type team inside the UK team.
finding: Public sources place OCIO and fiduciary management in Multi-Asset Solutions, an investing group, not inside a regional sales team [@R1-S15] [@R6-S18]. Its head is titled "Head of International OCIO and UK Fiduciary Management Team" [@R6-S04]. OCIO appears to have its own client relationship managers at senior level (snippet only) [@R1-S33]. A CSG-side sales seat for fiduciary management may still exist; that is not established either way.
use_in_interview: Describe OCIO as a business delivered by the multi-asset investment group that works with sales and relationship professionals.

claim: He is "pretty sure" OCIO exists only in the UK team.
finding: Goldman's OCIO business is global: $480bn of OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026, with large United States mandates announced in July 2026 [@R3-S09], a $40bn multi-country appointment in September 2025 that included Germany as well as the UK [@R3-S06], and an Irish fiduciary award in November 2026 [@R3-S11]. An OCIO insurance team works across The Hague, London and New York [@R1-S15]. What may be true is narrower: the UK is where the trustee-led "fiduciary management" market is most developed.
use_in_interview: Never say OCIO is UK-only. Say the UK is one of its largest markets.

topic: OCIO: taking on the client's team
claim: In OCIO, Goldman can bring the client's in-house investment team into the firm.
finding: True of the BAE Systems appointment: Goldman's press release says the schemes' in-house investment management team would join the firm [@R3-S01] [@R3-S02]. It is a feature of some very large mandates, not of the model in general: no transfer is reported for smaller UK fiduciary appointments [@R7-S15] [@R7-S16].
use_in_interview: Use as an example of one way a large mandate can be structured. Do not present it as how every OCIO appointment works.

claim: OCIO is already over-hired.
finding: No public support. The only public staffing evidence points the other way: a senior hire in September 2025 [@R6-S01] and a statement in November 2025 that the supporting multi-asset team of more than 300 was still growing [@R3-S07]. Neither says anything about analyst seats.
use_in_interview: Do not use, and do not let it steer which business you say interests you.

claim: Goldman recently won an OCIO award; he saw it in a LinkedIn post by a managing director.
finding: Two 2026 awards fit: Fiduciary Management / OCIO at the European Pensions Awards (2 July 2026) [@R3-S10] and Fiduciary Management / OCIO of the Year at the Irish Pensions Awards (4 November 2026) [@R3-S11]. Which one he saw is not established, and the managing director was not identified. Goldman did not win the fiduciary category at the 2026 UK Pensions Awards [@R3-S14]. An industry award shows that a judging panel rated an entry; it is not evidence of client outcomes.
use_in_interview: If you mention an award, name the awarding body and year, and do not lean on it as proof of quality.

claim: BAE Systems is an OCIO client, and that is confidential.
finding: The relationship is public, not confidential. Goldman's own press release of 6 September 2023 announced the appointment by the trustees of the BAE Systems pension schemes for about £23bn of defined benefit assets, after a competitive tender in which Redington advised the trustees [@R3-S01] [@R3-S02]. See [the mandate entry](#M-R7-01).
use_in_interview: Can be named, citing the press release. Attribute the decision to the trustees, and do not claim knowledge of the mandate beyond what was announced.

claim: A second named company is also an OCIO client, also described as confidential.
finding: No public source links Goldman to that company's pension schemes. The schemes' own latest annual reports name a different firm as fiduciary manager [@R3-S17] [@R3-S18]. The name is withheld from every output of this project.
use_in_interview: Never mention it. Repeating an unconfirmed client name in an interview would itself be a judgement failure.

claim: Arabic is not required for the Middle East team.
finding: The 2027 Dubai (CSG Third Party Wealth) and Doha (Alternatives Capital Formation, CSG) campus listings state no language requirement [@R1-S07] [@R1-S08]. No advertisement for London-based Middle East coverage was found, so the requirement for a London seat is not established.
use_in_interview: Reasonable to believe; do not assert it about the London team.

claim: He thinks the Middle East team is split into Third Party Wealth and Institutional.
finding: A Third Party Wealth sub-track is verified for Dubai [@R1-S07]. An institutional counterpart and any formal split were not found. The former head of the regional client business left in September 2025 and no successor was identified; his team was spread across London and Gulf offices [@R6-S14].
use_in_interview: Do not describe the team's internal structure.

claim: The Nordics team needs a local language.
finding: A London-based Nordics institutional sales support advertisement is reported as requiring native Swedish, but the page was seen only as a search summary [@R5-S08].
use_in_interview: Treat as probably true.

claim: The Switzerland team needs a local language.
finding: Mixed. A Zurich third-party wealth role is reported as requiring German [@R5-S11]. A London-based sales support advertisement for the Swiss client base shows no language requirement in the copy read [@R5-S06] [@R1-S18].
use_in_interview: Do not state a rule either way.

claim: The Benelux team needs a local language.
finding: "Native Dutch speaker is essential (written and oral fluency) with French an advantage", in the London-based BeNeLux Client Solutions Group advertisement live in October and November 2026 [@R1-S01].
use_in_interview: Accurate.

claim: Liquidity Solutions is a product line, not a region, with its own team because the product is strong. He did not know how it is split inside.
finding: Goldman presents Liquidity Solutions as a global business overseeing more than $1.2 trillion in money market and short-term assets, with global rather than regional leadership [@R5-S01] [@R5-S02]. An EMEA sales seat covering UK corporates is reported from a search summary [@R5-S09]. Its internal split is not published.
use_in_interview: Fine to describe it as a global product-line business with its own client base (treasurers and other cash holders).

claim: Everyone in Liquidity Solutions speaks French.
finding: No public evidence. The one French-speaker London advertisement found belongs to a French sales team, not to Liquidity Solutions [@R5-S10]. The transcript was garbled at this point, so the claim itself is uncertain.
use_in_interview: Do not use.

claim: Insurance is its own team with its own client base; where it sits in the structure is unclear.
finding: Goldman states it manages $651bn of general account assets for insurers and names global heads for the insurance business [@R5-S02]. Advertisement titles show an "Insurance Client Solutions Group" (snippet only) [@R1-S35]. It reads as a global client vertical that cuts across regions, not a regional team.
use_in_interview: Describe insurance as a global client specialism with constraints of its own (capital rules, matching liabilities).

claim: An English-only candidate is realistically limited to UK, Middle East and Liquidity Solutions.
finding: Directionally supported: every continental coverage advertisement read or summarised asked for a local language, while the UK third-party wealth advertisement asked for native English only [@R1-S17] [@R1-S01] [@R1-S05] [@R1-S06]. Insurance and consultant relations were not tested and may also be open to English-only candidates.
use_in_interview: Useful for your own expectations. It is not something to say in an interview.

claim: UK Institutional covers pension funds, endowments and foundations and sovereign wealth funds; pension funds dominate the work.
finding: Goldman's EMEA institutional marketing advertisement defines the institutional business as pension funds, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds and insurers [@R1-S20]. That pension funds dominate the UK work is plausible given the size of UK pension assets but is not stated by any Goldman source.
use_in_interview: The client list is safe. Present the weight of pensions as your reasoning, not as a fact about the team.

topic: Third Party Wealth: what it does
claim: Third Party Wealth sells Goldman funds to other wealth managers and private banks, which offer them to their own clients. His example was a fund sold to a named private bank.
finding: The description matches Goldman's wording: the UK TPW Sales Team is responsible for new business development with "private banks, wealth managers, financial advisors and multi-managers" [@R1-S17], and a press release names an "EMEA Third Party Wealth Business" [@R4-S01]. His named example is his own illustration and has no public source.
use_in_interview: Use the description. Do not repeat the named example as a real relationship.

topic: Private Wealth Management as a buyer
claim: Goldman's own Private Wealth Management buys other managers' funds, which makes it a third-party wealth client for firms like Pictet.
finding: Goldman's Private Wealth Management site describes an open-architecture alternatives platform that includes external managers [@R4-S27]. So the general point holds for alternatives. Whether any particular external manager is on that platform is not public.
use_in_interview: Useful for seeing the business from the buyer's side. Name no external manager.

claim: Within each team the sales side is called CSG and the relationship-management side is called CCG (Client Coverage Group).
finding: "Client Coverage Group (CCG)" is a real Goldman name, defined as the group "dedicated to retaining, expanding and supporting existing client relationships" [@R1-S11]. But a London CSG team is described as doing both new business and existing relationships [@R1-S01], and no public source shows London teams using the two acronyms for two sides of one desk, or shows whether CCG sits inside CSG. London CCG titles were seen in snippets only [@R1-S32].
use_in_interview: Describe the two kinds of work and ask how the team splits them. Do not assert the acronyms as fact.

claim: "CSG" means two things: the whole umbrella group and the sales side within a team.
finding: The first meaning is verified ("Global Client Solutions Group") [@R1-S13]. The loose use as a synonym for sales is verified in titles [@R1-S09]. The specific second meaning he gave, a label for one side of a team, is not shown publicly.
use_in_interview: Be explicit about which sense you mean when you use the term.

claim: Analyst base salary is £52k on the sales side and £48k on the relationship side; sales bonuses are larger and the gap widens with seniority.
finding: No credible public source gives London pay for these roles. Goldman's careers listings leave the salary field empty for the EMEA roles read. The only official figures are United States pay-transparency ranges for non-client-facing CSG roles [@R1-S13] [@R1-S30], which cannot be read across.
use_in_interview: Never raise it. Do not treat a reported £4k difference as evidence of prestige or role quality.

claim: Sales has fewer seats and is harder to get; relationship management has more.
finding: No headcount by function is published. In the public people sample, explicitly sales-titled people outnumber explicitly relationship-titled people, but that reflects which appointments get announced, not staffing [@R6-S17] [@R6-S27].
use_in_interview: Do not use. It should not decide which side you say you prefer.

claim: The two sides sit opposite each other, work the same hours and operate as one team; at analyst level the work is basically the same.
finding: Nothing public describes seating or hours. It is consistent with the BeNeLux advertisement, where one junior role supports both new business and existing relationships [@R1-S01].
use_in_interview: Reasonable background for your own expectations. If you refer to it, say a former intern described it that way.

claim: Sales is seen as more prestigious; many relationship people want to move across; internal moves are bureaucratic.
finding: One person's impression of culture. Nothing public supports or contradicts it.
use_in_interview: Do not use. Expressing a preference because one side is "more prestigious" would be a weak reason in any case.

claim: A managing director posted about the OCIO award; a partner told him assessment centres are moving in person and will ask more about AI.
finding: Neither person could be identified from public sources and no identity is suggested here. The Partner Class of 2026 lists Asset & Wealth Management partners in London but does not say which business each works in [@R1-S27].
use_in_interview: Do not try to name either person.

claim: The first stage is a recorded video interview.
finding: Goldman's own steps page: "you will be asked to participate in a video interview, which will take approximately 30 minutes to complete", referred to as the HireVue interview [@R1-S23].
use_in_interview: Prepare for a recorded format.

claim: An associate on the team reviews the recorded video, sometimes at double speed.
finding: Nothing public says who reviews recordings or how.
use_in_interview: The only sensible lesson is general: make the first sentences of an answer clear. Build no tactic on it.

claim: What you say in the recorded interview decides which team you are "drafted" to: region, client type, and sales or relationship management.
finding: The mechanism is not published. The 2027 London listing names no sub-track while Frankfurt, Paris and Dubai listings do [@R1-S05] [@R1-S06] [@R1-S07], so some allocation must happen after applying, but how is unknown.
use_in_interview: Do not plant keywords to steer allocation. Talk about the client segments that actually interest you and say why.

claim: The assessment centre is three back-to-back interviews with the team and no group task: analyst and associate together, then a vice president or similar, then the managing director who runs the team.
finding: Officially the final round ("Superday") is "between two and five interviews for campus hires, depending on the division" with "a cross-section of people whom you could possibly work with" [@R1-S23]. Three interviews fits inside that range. The number, order, interviewers and absence of a group task are his experience of one team in one year. "Vice president or similar" fits the fact that Executive Director is the same level as Vice President in EMEA [@R1-S26].
use_in_interview: Prepare for several one-to-one or two-to-one interviews with team members at different levels; do not rely on the exact sequence.

claim: Assessment centres are now in person and will ask more about AI.
finding: Official pages read are silent on both. Press coverage was not searched because the search allowance ran out, so this is "not investigated" beyond official sources. Recruiters' published guidance says questions are "situational or behavioral" and that they weigh "attitude and aptitude" [@R1-S24].
use_in_interview: Be ready for either format, and have a considered view on how AI changes client work (see the commercial-awareness chapter). Confirm the format with your recruiter.

claim: Each team hires one analyst per open seat, so a candidate competes only against others drafted to the same team.
finding: Nothing public describes seat numbers or how candidates are compared. No hiring probability can be inferred.
use_in_interview: Do not use.

claim: Each team runs its own hiring timeline, so offers on one team say nothing about another.
finding: Goldman says it evaluates applications throughout the season and that candidates "may hear back regarding different roles at different times" [@R1-S23]. That is about roles, not teams within one listing, so it is consistent with the claim without confirming it.
use_in_interview: Useful for managing your own expectations only.

claim: Asset management is about 30% of Goldman's revenue and valued for stable fee income.
finding: The figure matches the Asset & Wealth Management segment, which was 28.6% of firmwide net revenues in 2025. The Asset Management business on its own was 11.6% [@R2-S01]. Management and other fees were $11,538m, 69% of the segment, which is the fee income the "stable" point refers to. Fees recur while clients stay and markets hold; they are not guaranteed. Nothing is disclosed for the Client Solutions Group.
use_in_interview: Say "Asset & Wealth Management was about 29% of 2025 net revenues" and name the segment. Do not say asset management alone is 30%.

claim: Goldman recently restricted staff use of Claude Code.
finding: Bloomberg reported on 2 November 2026 that Goldman restricted traders and bankers from some AI tools; outlets relaying it say internal guidance limited Claude Code and GitHub's AI coding tools to engineers [@R2-S10] [@R2-S08] [@R2-S09]. The Bloomberg article itself could not be read. It is one report, it concerns coding tools for non-engineers, it is not a firm-wide ban on AI, and nothing says how it applies to asset-management client staff. A separate April 2026 report concerned Hong Kong bankers' access to one model [@R2-S12].
use_in_interview: If AI comes up, describe it accurately as a reported restriction of coding tools to engineers, citing the press. Do not call it a ban on AI.

claim: Details about the former intern's own background, his friend's internship and a candidate he knows.
finding: Not researched, by design. These are private individuals and nothing about them is needed to understand the business.
use_in_interview: Not relevant. Do not name him or rely on "someone told me" as support for any claim.

claim: An English-only UK candidate is most likely to be sent to the UK team, with the Middle East possible if the answers mention the Middle East.
finding: No public information on allocation. See IC-36.
use_in_interview: Do not mention a region you have no real interest in to influence allocation. If the Gulf's sovereign investors do interest you, say why in terms of the clients.
